Molecular Cytogenetics of Cancer

Pat Schoenlein, Ph.D. • Tuesday Lecture 3 • Week 5: Foundations of Cancer Biology

🔥 Professor-emphasis map

This lecture contains extensive red, yellow, green, and underlined emphasis. I prioritized those points rather than treating every slide detail equally.

  • BCL2 overexpression can produce multidrug resistance (MDR) because chemotherapy may fail to activate the intrinsic apoptotic pathway.
  • t(14;18) → BCL2 overexpression in follicular/B-cell lymphoma; the lecture repeatedly connects this translocation to resistance to chemotherapy.
  • t(9;22) → BCR-ABL on the Philadelphia chromosome → constitutively active tyrosine kinase driving CML.
  • Detection sensitivity increases from karyotype → FISH → quantitative RT-PCR for BCR-ABL in the lecture.
  • Genomic instability is a hallmark of cancer and includes translocations, deletions, aneuploidy, and gene amplification.
  • p53/RB checkpoint loss promotes genomic instability. p53 is presented as the “guardian of the genome.”
  • Gene amplification can be intrachromosomal (HSR/ABR) or extrachromosomal (double minutes).
  • CCND1/Cyclin D1, MDM2, MYCN, and HER2/neu are the four required amplification examples.
  • MYCN amplification = poor-prognosis neuroblastoma.
  • HER2 amplification predicts aggressive biology but also creates a targetable vulnerability.

Learning Objectives

  1. Identify MDR by understanding how BCL2 can inhibit standard cancer therapies and how BCL2 translocation can cause BCL2 overexpression.
  2. Explain chromosomal translocations in cancer cells using BCL2 and BCR-ABL as major examples.
  3. Explain genomic instability, gene amplification, and p53 as the “guardian of the genome.”
  4. Describe the significance of amplification of Cyclin D in breast/bladder cancer, MDM2 in sarcomas, MYCN in neuroblastoma, and HER2/neu in breast cancer relative to survival and treatment options.
Contents
  1. LO1 - BCL2, apoptosis, and multidrug resistance
  2. LO2 - Cancer translocations: t(14;18) and t(9;22)
  3. CML and BCR-ABL detection
  4. LO3 - Genomic instability and p53

LO1 - BCL2, Intrinsic Apoptosis, and Multidrug Resistance

Core idea: many anticancer therapies ultimately depend on the tumor cell’s ability to execute apoptosis. If anti-apoptotic BCL2 is highly expressed, the cell can survive multiple structurally unrelated drugs.

Intrinsic mitochondrial apoptosis

  • Cytotoxic or intracellular stress activates pro-apoptotic signals.
  • BH3-only proteins such as BIM can oppose anti-apoptotic BCL2-family proteins and favor activation of BAX/BAK.
  • BAX/BAK promote mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilization → cytochrome c release → APAF-1/caspase-9 → effector caspases → apoptosis.
  • BCL2 is anti-apoptotic. High BCL2 shifts the balance toward survival.
Lecture p. 3 - review of the intrinsic apoptosis pathway. The professor highlights BCL2/BIM/BAX interactions and the connection to MDR.

What “multidrug resistance” means here

  • MDR means resistance to multiple drugs that differ in structure and function.
  • The lecture’s key mechanism is failure to trigger the intrinsic apoptosis pathway.
  • BCL2 overexpression is one mechanism; p53 loss can also contribute because BAX and other death-inducing genes are not appropriately activated.
🔥 PROFESSOR EMPHASIS

BCL2 overexpression → resistance to apoptosis → resistance to multiple chemotherapeutic agents. The lecture uses this as a mechanistic definition of MDR.

⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD - Another classic MDR mechanism

Board resources also emphasize MDR1/P-glycoprotein (ABCB1), an ATP-dependent drug-efflux pump that lowers intracellular concentrations of many chemotherapeutic agents. This is a separate mechanism from the BCL2-based apoptosis resistance emphasized in this lecture.

⚠️ COMMONLY CONFUSED

BCL2 overexpression does not primarily increase proliferation. Its classic effect is preventing cell death. A tumor can therefore accumulate because cells live too long, even without a dramatic increase in mitotic rate.

LO2 - Chromosomal Translocations in Cancer

Core idea: reciprocal translocations exchange DNA between nonhomologous chromosomes. Cancer can result when a translocation places a gene under a powerful regulatory element or creates a new oncogenic fusion protein.

Basic translocation terminology

  • A chromosomal translocation is an exchange of chromosomal material between nonhomologous chromosomes.
  • A reciprocal translocation creates two derivative (der) chromosomes.
  • Each derivative chromosome is named for the chromosome that contributed its centromere.
  • A breakpoint is the site where chromosomal continuity changes and foreign chromosomal material begins.

BCL2 translocation: t(14;18)

In follicular lymphoma, BCL2 on chromosome 18 is translocated near the immunoglobulin heavy-chain regulatory region on chromosome 14. The result is abnormally high BCL2 expression and resistance to apoptosis.

Lecture p. 7 - t(14;18) causes high-level BCL2 expression and is linked in the lecture to chemotherapy resistance.
⚠️ LECTURE WORDING VS BOARD WORDING

The lecture describes BCL2 as coming under an “IgG promoter.” The standard board framing is that BCL2 is juxtaposed to the IGH regulatory/enhancer region at 14q32. The tested consequence is the same: constitutive BCL2 overexpression.

FISH detection of t(14;18)

Lecture p. 9 - dual-color, dual-fusion FISH uses locus-specific probes for the IGH region on chromosome 14 and BCL2 on chromosome 18.

BCR-ABL translocation: t(9;22)

A reciprocal translocation joins ABL1 from chromosome 9 with BCR on chromosome 22, forming the Philadelphia chromosome and a constitutively active BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase.

Lecture p. 10 - t(9;22) creates BCR-ABL; the highlighted text emphasizes constitutive ABL kinase signaling.
⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD - BCL2 vs BCR-ABL
TranslocationWhat it doesClassic cancer
t(14;18)Overexpresses anti-apoptotic BCL2Follicular lymphoma
t(9;22)Creates constitutively active BCR-ABL tyrosine kinaseCML; also a subset of ALL

CML and BCR-ABL Detection

The lecture presents CML as a myeloproliferative disorder with increased granulocytic cells and their immature precursors while retaining the ability to differentiate.

Clinical clues emphasized in the lecture

  • Elevated WBC count with granulocytes and immature precursors.
  • Fatigue, weight loss, low-grade fever, sweating.
  • Splenomegaly → early satiety, LUQ discomfort/pain.
  • Progression through chronic, accelerated, and blast phases.
Lecture p. 13 - FISH can detect co-localization/fusion of BCR and ABL signals in interphase cells.

Detection sensitivity in the lecture

MethodWhat it detectsLecture sensitivity
KaryotypePhiladelphia chromosome in metaphase cells~1 in 20
FISHBCR-ABL fusion using locus-specific probes~1 in 250
Quantitative RT-PCRBCR-ABL transcript level~1 in 105-106
Lecture p. 15 / handout p. 58. Treat the exact ratios as lecture-specific figures; the important concept is the increasing molecular sensitivity.
⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD - CML

Classic board clues include marked leukocytosis with left-shifted granulocytes, basophilia, splenomegaly, and low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP). BCR-ABL is a constitutively active nonreceptor tyrosine kinase and is targeted by ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib.

LO3 - Genomic Instability and p53, the “Guardian of the Genome”

Core idea: genomic instability means a cancer cell has an increased tendency to accumulate DNA mutations and numerical/structural chromosome abnormalities during cell division.
Lecture p. 17 - translocations, deletions, and gene amplifications are highlighted as frequent manifestations of genomic instability.

Why instability develops

  • Normal checkpoints prevent cells with major DNA or chromosome damage from continuing through the cell cycle.
  • Loss of p53, RB, or related checkpoint/repair functions permits damaged cells to survive and divide.
  • The lecture connects checkpoint loss to increased gene amplification, chromosome deletion, and aneuploidy.
🔥 LECTURE-SPECIFIC STATISTIC

The lecture states that “at least 90% of all cancers have lost p53 or RB function.” Treat this as a lecture emphasis on the centrality of these checkpoint pathways, not as a general board statistic you need to memorize literally.

p53 mechanism worth knowing

  • DNA damage activates p53.
  • p53 can increase p21 → CDK inhibition → cell-cycle arrest, giving the cell time to repair DNA.
  • If damage is irreparable, p53 can promote apoptosis, including induction of pro-apoptotic genes such as BAX.
  • Loss of p53 therefore contributes to both genomic instability and therapy resistance.
⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD - p53 and MDM2

MDM2 is a negative regulator of p53. MDM2 ubiquitinates p53 and promotes its proteasomal degradation. MDM2 amplification can therefore create a functional “p53-null” phenotype even when the TP53 gene itself is not deleted.

Gene Amplification: Amplicons, HSRs, and Double Minutes

Definition

  • Gene amplification means one or more genes are present at a copy number greater than the normal 2n state.
  • It often follows complex recombination plus repeated replication of a DNA segment.
  • The repeating amplified DNA unit is the amplicon and often contains more than one gene.
  • Amplification is maintained when it provides a selective growth or survival advantage.
TypeWhere amplified DNA is foundKey morphology
Intrachromosomal amplificationWithin a chromosomeHSR (homogeneously staining region) / ABR in lecture terminology
Extrachromosomal amplificationOutside normal chromosomesDouble-minute chromosomes (DMs/dmins), small acentric DNA elements
Lecture p. 22 - double minutes contain replication origins but lack centromeres, so they can segregate unevenly between daughter cells.
⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD - Why double minutes matter

Because DMs are acentric and segregate unevenly, different daughter cells can receive different oncogene copy numbers. This contributes to intratumoral heterogeneity and can facilitate treatment resistance.

LOW PRIORITY / FYI IN LECTURE

The detailed mechanisms of double-minute formation, chromosome territories, and extrachromosomal circular-DNA biology are explicitly labeled FYI only in the lecture. Understand the concept; do not over-memorize the mechanistic details.

LO4 - Required Gene-Amplification Examples

1. CCND1 / Cyclin D1 amplification

Amplified Cyclin D1 binds and activates CDK4/6 → RB phosphorylation/inactivation → release of E2F → G1-to-S progression continues unchecked.

Lecture p. 29 - the highlighted clinical point connects Cyclin D upregulation to loss of the RB restriction point and development of CDK4/6 inhibitors.
  • Lecture examples: breast cancer and bladder cancer.
  • CCND1 status is presented as a potential prognostic/predictive marker in bladder cancer.
  • Amplified Cyclin D1 behaves as an oncogenic driver.
⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD - Cyclin D distinction

Do not confuse CCND1 amplification with the classic t(11;14) Cyclin D1 translocation in mantle cell lymphoma. Both increase Cyclin D1 activity, but the cytogenetic mechanism differs.

2. MDM2 amplification

MDM2 amplification is emphasized in sarcomas, especially tumors such as liposarcoma. MDM2 is a ubiquitin ligase that promotes p53 destruction.

Lecture p. 32 - increased MDM2 suppresses the tumor-suppressor function of p53.
Lecture p. 35 - dual-color FISH: many MDM2 signals compared with the chromosome 12 centromere control demonstrate amplification.
  • MDM2 amplification can produce a functional p53-null phenotype.
  • This weakens checkpoint control, DNA-damage responses, and apoptosis.
  • The lecture connects MDM2/p53 dysfunction to MDR through failure to induce death-promoting genes.
🩺 CLINICAL CONNECTION

The lecture notes that proteasome activity is a therapeutic target in some hematologic malignancies and names bortezomib as an example. This is adjacent to, but not the central focus of, the MDM2 learning objective.

3. MYCN amplification in neuroblastoma

  • MYCN (N-MYC) is a proto-oncogenic transcription factor involved in cell growth and proliferation.
  • Neuroblastoma arises from neural crest-derived sympathetic nervous system tissue, often in the adrenal region.
  • The lecture states that MYCN amplification occurs in a subset of patients and is associated with the poorest prognosis.
  • MYCN amplification is commonly shown as intrachromosomal HSR/ABR amplification in this lecture.
Lecture p. 42 - amplified MYCN is presented as an oncogenic driver of neuroblastoma growth.
⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD - Neuroblastoma

Classic board clues include a young child with an adrenal/sympathetic-chain mass that can cross the midline, elevated urinary HVA/VMA, and sometimes opsoclonus-myoclonus. MYCN amplification is a high-risk/poor-prognostic feature.

⚠️ COMMONLY CONFUSED - MYC vs MYCN

MYC (c-MYC) is classically activated by t(8;14) in Burkitt lymphoma.
MYCN (N-MYC) amplification is classically associated with neuroblastoma.

4. HER2/neu (ERBB2) amplification in breast cancer

HER2 is a receptor tyrosine kinase. Amplification/overexpression increases growth and survival signaling through pathways including RAS-MEK and PI3K-AKT.

Lecture p. 45 - HER2 amplification drives survival/proliferative signaling and contributes to drug resistance.

How amplification is detected

Lecture p. 46 - locus-specific FISH detects multiple HER2 DNA signals in breast-cancer nuclei.
TestWhat it asks
IHCIs HER2 protein overexpressed on the tumor-cell membrane?
FISH / ISHIs the ERBB2/HER2 gene amplified?
⚠️ COMMONLY CONFUSED - Protein vs gene

IHC measures protein expression. FISH/ISH measures gene amplification. They are related but are not the same assay.

Prognosis and targeted therapy

  • The lecture links HER2 amplification to early recurrence / more aggressive behavior.
  • HER2 amplification also creates a targetable abnormality.
  • Trastuzumab (Herceptin) is the major antibody example in the lecture.
  • The lecture also notes small-molecule HER2 tyrosine kinase inhibitors.
Lecture p. 49 - HER2 amplification demonstrated by FISH leads directly to a targeted-therapy concept.
⭐ STEP 1 HIGH YIELD - HER2 therapy

Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody against HER2/ERBB2 and is classically associated with cardiotoxicity/dilated cardiomyopathy. Modern HER2-directed therapy also includes additional antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates, and small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

🔥 LECTURE NUMBER CAUTION

The lecture gives HER2-positive/overexpressing breast-cancer proportions ranging from roughly 15-30% and one slide states ~30%. Do not make the exact percentage your main memorization target. The high-yield concept is HER2 amplification/overexpression → aggressive biology + eligibility for HER2-directed therapy.

LOW PRIORITY / FYI IN LECTURE

The blood-brain barrier limitation of trastuzumab and proposed workarounds are presented as FYI/forward-looking material. Know that large monoclonal antibodies have limited CNS penetration; do not prioritize the detailed delivery discussion for this lecture.

Rapid Step 1 Review Sheet

BCL2

Anti-apoptotic protein; t(14;18) → follicular lymphoma.

MDR

Resistance to multiple unrelated drugs; lecture mechanism = blocked intrinsic apoptosis.

BCR-ABL

t(9;22), constitutively active tyrosine kinase, CML.

CML therapy

ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor such as imatinib.

Genomic instability

Increased mutations + chromosome abnormalities: translocations, deletions, amplification, aneuploidy.

p53

DNA-damage checkpoint; p21 arrest + apoptosis when damage is severe.

MDM2

Ubiquitin ligase that degrades p53; amplification can phenocopy p53 loss.

HSR

Intrachromosomal gene amplification.

Double minute

Extrachromosomal amplified DNA; acentric; uneven segregation.

CCND1

Cyclin D1 → CDK4/6 → RB phosphorylation → E2F → S phase.

MYCN

Neuroblastoma amplification; poor/high-risk prognostic feature.

HER2

ERBB2 receptor tyrosine kinase amplification in breast cancer; targetable.

HER2 testing

IHC = protein; FISH/ISH = gene amplification.

Trastuzumab

Anti-HER2 monoclonal antibody; cardiomyopathy risk.

Highest-priority “can you explain it out loud?” list

  1. How BCL2 blocks intrinsic apoptosis and why that can create multidrug resistance.
  2. Why t(14;18) causes BCL2 overexpression rather than a fusion tyrosine kinase.
  3. Why t(9;22) creates a constitutively active BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase.
  4. How karyotype, FISH, and RT-PCR differ conceptually for BCR-ABL detection.
  5. What genomic instability means and why p53/RB loss promotes it.
  6. How p53 normally responds to DNA damage through p21 arrest and apoptosis.
  7. What gene amplification is and the difference between HSRs and double minutes.
  8. How Cyclin D1 amplification drives G1→S progression through CDK4/6-RB-E2F.
  9. How MDM2 amplification functionally suppresses p53 and can contribute to MDR.
  10. Why MYCN amplification is important in neuroblastoma.
  11. How HER2 amplification is detected and why it changes both prognosis and treatment.
  12. The difference between IHC protein overexpression and FISH gene amplification.
